Advanced workflow

Source: vignettes/advanced-workflow.Rmd
advanced-workflow.Rmd
library(InterPlotComp)

This vignette covers the three things that turn a working single-trial fit into a production analysis: a relationship matrix, a covariate for the physical cause of interference, and the multi-environment model.

It assumes you have read Basic workflow.

Multi-environment trials

A series of environments is prepared through the same function, with multi_env = TRUE and an environment column mapped:

met_raw <- sample_met_trial()
table(met_raw$Environment)
#> 
#> Env01 Env02 Env03 Env04 
#>   108   111   100   120

met <- prepare_trial_data(
  met_raw,
  map = list(yield = "Yield_t_ha", geno = "Genotype", row = "Row",
             column = "Column", env = "Environment", rep = "Rep",
             block = "Block"),
  multi_env = TRUE
)

attr(met, "field_summary")
#>   Environment Rows Columns    Grid Plots Observed Missing_response Gaps_in_grid
#> 1       Env01   12       9  12 × 9   108      107                1            0
#> 2       Env02   14       8  14 × 8   111      109                2            1
#> 3       Env03   10      10 10 × 10   100       99                1            0
#> 4       Env04   12      10 12 × 10   120      118                2            0
#>   Genotypes Min_reps Max_reps Unreplicated
#> 1        40        2        4            0
#> 2        44        2        4            0
#> 3        40        2        5            0
#> 4        48        2        6            0

The four environments have different sizes, different genotype panels and unequal replication — which is what a real series looks like. Each is padded to its own rectangle and gets its own residual section:

met_nb <- add_neighbours(complete_field_grid(met), axis = "rows")
nlevels(met_nb$data$Env)
#> [1] 4

Design factors are nested inside environment automatically. Block “1” in one environment is not the same block as “1” in another, and collapsing them is a common cause of a singular Average Information matrix:

head(levels(met_nb$data$RepF))
#> [1] "Env01:1" "Env02:1" "Env03:1" "Env04:1" "Env01:2" "Env02:2"

Choosing the between-environment structure

structure What it assumes Parameters
"diag" No genetic correlation between environments fewest
"facv" Joint factor-analytic covariance over direct and competitive effects most
"separable" One 2×2 direct–competition covariance crossed with one environment covariance middle
"fa" Separate FA covariances; direct–competition covariance fixed at zero middle

"facv" is the model you want if it will fit: it is the only one that lets the direct–competition covariance differ between environments. "separable" is the usual fallback, costing 3 + E(r + 1) parameters instead of 2E(r + 1).

met_fit <- fit_met_model(
  met_nb$data, met_nb$names,
  opts = list(structure = "facv", rank = 1L, spatial = TRUE, nugget = FALSE,
              auto_simplify = TRUE, exact_se = FALSE, cinv_limit = 0L,
              maxit = 25L, workspace = "2gb", compare_baseline = FALSE,
              max_rounds = 10L)
)

met_fit$converged
met_fit$description

Genetic correlations between environments 

round(met_fit$matrices$direct_cor, 3)

These are the correlations that decide whether one selection serves all environments. Values near 1 mean a genotype that wins in one environment wins in the others; values near zero mean environment-specific recommendations.

plot_correlation_heatmap(met_fit$matrices$direct_cor,
                         title = "Direct effects")
met_fit$variance

Stability across environments 

plot_stability(met_fit$values, top_n = 10)

Lines that stay parallel are stable genotypes. Lines that cross are crossover genotype-by-environment interaction, and mean the recommendation depends on the environment.

Pedigree and genomic relationships

By default genetic effects are independent between genotypes. Supplying a relationship matrix replaces that with a known covariance between relatives. For a competition model this matters twice over: the competitive effect is the harder of the two to estimate, and it borrows most of its information from relatives.

Three sources are accepted — a pedigree, a ready-made kinship matrix, or a marker matrix:

ped <- sample_pedigree()
head(ped)

rel <- build_relationship(
  type = "pedigree",
  raw  = ped,
  map  = list(id = "Genotype", sire = "Male_parent", dam = "Female_parent")
)

rel$label
rel$diagnostics[c("n", "n_founders")]

A marker matrix goes through VanRaden’s method 1, with a small ridge blended in so the result can be inverted:

rel <- build_relationship("markers", raw = my_marker_data, blend = 0.01)

Pass the result to either fitting function:

nb <- add_neighbours(
  complete_field_grid(
    prepare_trial_data(sample_single_trial(),
                       list(yield = "Yield_t_ha", geno = "Genotype",
                            row = "Row", column = "Column", rep = "Rep"))),
  axis = "rows")

rel_fit <- fit_single_model(
  nb$data, nb$names,
  opts = list(structure = "diag", spatial = TRUE, nugget = FALSE,
              auto_simplify = TRUE, exact_se = FALSE, cinv_limit = 0L,
              maxit = 25L, workspace = "1gb", compare_baseline = FALSE,
              max_rounds = 10L, relationship = rel)
)

rel_fit$coverage

Individuals in the relationship matrix with no plot in the trial — ancestors, untested relatives — are kept, and their effects are predicted from their relatives and flagged:

table(rel_fit$genetic$Tested)

Every genotype with an observed plot must appear in the relationship matrix. If one does not, the fit stops and names it rather than dropping it silently.

Adjusting for a covariate

Interference has a physical cause — plant height, canopy width, root vigour. If you measured it, you can ask how much of the competitive effect it explains. The covariate enters as a fixed effect twice: once for the plot’s own value and once summed over exactly the neighbours that supply the competitive effects.

cov_prepared <- prepare_trial_data(
  sample_single_trial(),
  list(yield = "Yield_t_ha", geno = "Genotype", row = "Row",
       column = "Column", rep = "Rep", covariate = "Plant_height_cm")
)
cov_nb <- add_neighbours(complete_field_grid(cov_prepared), "rows")

cov_fit <- fit_single_model(
  cov_nb$data, cov_nb$names,
  opts = list(structure = "diag", spatial = TRUE, nugget = FALSE,
              auto_simplify = TRUE, exact_se = FALSE, cinv_limit = 0L,
              maxit = 25L, workspace = "1gb", compare_baseline = FALSE,
              max_rounds = 10L, adjust_own_covariate = TRUE)
)

cov_fit$covariate_terms
cov_fit$wald

The covariate is centred, so the intercept stays the fitted mean at an average covariate value and predicted pure-stand yields remain on the scale a breeder expects. A covariate that is missing for more than half the plots is refused: adjusting for something mostly absent biases the competitive effects more than it corrects them.

The simplification ladder

Both fitting functions take auto_simplify. When TRUE, a specification that will not converge is replaced by the next model down a nested ladder, giving up the least defensible assumption first:

  1. a second-order residual process, back to AR1 × AR1;
  2. the us(2) covariance, reparameterised as corgh(2);
  3. the independent nugget variance;
  4. the direct–competition covariance, constrained to zero;
  5. the block and then replicate variances;
  6. the spatial residual — last, because dropping it biases everything else.
met_fit$log

Always read this log. A result from step 4 is a different scientific claim from a result at step 1, and the difference belongs in your methods section.

Reproducible scripting

Nothing above needs the Shiny interface. A complete analysis is:

library(InterPlotComp)

d  <- prepare_trial_data(read.csv("trial.csv"), map = my_map)
d  <- complete_field_grid(d)
nb <- add_neighbours(d, "rows")
fit <- fit_single_model(nb$data, nb$names, opts = my_opts)

write.csv(fit$genetic, "genotype_values.csv", row.names = FALSE)
